newsitem.title: CHINA: Deng changed lives of China's 800 million farmers.
newsitem.headline: Deng changed lives of China's 800 million farmers.

text.p: Few Chinese had their lives changed more by paramount leader Deng Xiaoping than the country's 800 million peasants.
Deng, who died on Wednesday, allowed them to farm their own land, to sell much of their produce at market prices and to set up factories and enterprises to employ those no longer needed on the farms.
The result was a dramatic increase in farm output and the birth of a burgeoning industrial sector in the countryside that employs millions of people.

But Deng's successes did not solve China's farm problems. Investment in agriculture is a fraction of that in real estate or industry, most farming remains small-scale and inefficient, and per capita arable land is shrinking.
The communists took power in 1949 by mobilising farmers with a promise they would receive land confiscated from landlords.
But they broke their promise and collectivised agriculture in the mid-1950s, putting farmers in "people's communes" where they received the same pay however much or little they worked.
Output grew slowly.

In 1978, the last year of the pre-Deng era, grain output was 304.70 million tonnes, with a per capita output of 317 kg (697 lb), against 164 million tonnes in 1952 when per capita output was 285 kg (627 lb).

Deng revolutionised agricultural policy after he took power, scrapping communes and allowing farmers to have their own plots on long-term leases while gradually liberalising prices of most farm goods so that they were set by the market.
In 1984, grain output leapt to 407.31 million tonnes, with a per capita output of 390 kg (858 lb), and cotton output reached a record 6.26 million tonnes from 2.167 million in 1978.

This higher agricultural output both enriched farmers and ended rationing for urban residents, who were able to buy from free markets or state shops, instead of queuing with ration coupons as in the days of the late chairman Mao Zedong.
Deng's reforms ended state monopolies on the purchase, distribution and sale of most farm products, leaving just three still under state monopoly -- cotton, silk and tobacco.
Deng encouraged the establishment of factories and businesses in rural areas, which employ more than 120 million people and are major contributors to export earnings.
He also ended Mao's ban on movement of farmers from their villages, allowing them to seek work in nearby towns or distant cities.
But Deng could not solve all of China's age-old farm problems.
"The major success of Deng's farm reforms came in the 1978-84 period when output soared and the income gap between farmers and city people narrowed," said one Chinese economist.

"After 1984, increases in farm output slowed, while the urban economy continued to grow fast, so the income gap began to widen again. Costs of pesticides and fertiliser soared. Village enterprises did not grow fast enough to absorb the excess labour, which started to move to the cities," he said.
Most farming remains small-scale, labour-intensive and inefficient, attracting little investment from home or abroad.
As a result of a doubling of the population since 1949, per capita arable land has fallen to less than 0.08 hectares (0.2 acres) from 0.18 hectares (0.44 acres) in 1953.
Corruption remains widespread among rural officials who siphon off money budgeted for agriculture and impose illegal taxes and levies on farmers.
Under Deng, farm incomes grew but still lagged earnings of urban residents. The richest 20 percent of Chinese -- in the cities -- now earn 60 times that of the poorest 20 percent -- on the farms.
